ba-1934-cosmo.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 20 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled coupe
4. Garnish with an orange twist
ba-1934-cosmo.description: A simple sour can be so different with the right base spirit. The 1934 Cosmo hits its stride with a complex and floral gin. Grab a bottle whose botanicals include multiple berries and flowers. We'd suggest Monkey 47.

ba-2-to-2.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 10 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled glass
4. Garnish with an orange peel
ba-2-to-2.description: A bittersweet cocktail that's more accessible than its ingredient list may suggest.

ba-20th-century.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients with ice and shake
2. Strain into a coupe, serve up
ba-20th-century.description: The 20th Century is a cocktail created in 1937 by a British bartender named C.A. Tuck, and named in honor of the celebrated 20th Century Limited train which ran between New York City and Chicago from 1902 until 1967.

ba-212.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a shaker and shake
2. Double strain into large, chilled glass filled with ice.
3. Optionally top with soda.
ba-212.description: The 212 is a delectable cocktail in a big, beautiful, reddish-pink package. It’s a simple summer diddy that wins hearts with a kiss of bitterness and a big splash of earthy fruit. The recipe was originally conceived by Aisha Sharpe and Willy Shine of the cocktail consultancy Contemporary Cocktails, who created menus and drinks for NYC hot spots. It later found its way into the fabulous PDT Cocktail Book, and a wider distribution of eyes and tongues. The name is both a reference to Manhattan’s most popular area code as well as the ratios in the drink, which if you ask us, is pretty freaking clever.
ba-212.garnish: grapefruit peel or orange peel for garnish

ba-21st-and-14-century.method_text:
1. Add all of the ingredients to the shaker with ice and shake to chill.
2. Strain into a glass, then garnish.
ba-21st-and-14-century.description: This twist on the 20th Century cocktail uses coconut rum as a stand-in for gin, a sub that works seamlessly with the drink's lemon and crème de cacao. "I dig the coconut-chocolate-citrus combo," says the recipe's creator, Erik Tennyson.

ba-8-amaro-sazerac.method_text: Stir with ice, strain into a rocks glass pre-rinsed with Green Chartreuse, and garnish with a lemon twist.
ba-8-amaro-sazerac.description: Mayur Subbarao created this recipe for the opening menu at Manhattan's Amor y Amargo in 2011, and it has remained on the list there ever since.

ba-absent-stars.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 20 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled rocks glass
ba-absent-stars.description: A nouveau tropical rum cocktail with big passionfruit and grapefruit flavor. From Nick Detrich.

ba-absinthe-colada.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 10 seconds
3. Strain into a hurricane glass filled with crushed ice
ba-absinthe-colada.description: Mint and coconut are an excellent pairing that's underused in cocktails. This piña colada variant from Maison Premiere in Brooklyn employs mint in two ways in this boldly flavored cocktail.

ba-absinthe-frappe.method_text:
1. Combine syrup and absinthe in a shaker filled with ice
2. Shake for 10 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled glass filled with crushed ice
ba-absinthe-frappe.description: A dreamy classic that makes absinthe approachable and surprisingly refreshing.

ba-absinthe-old-fashioned.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients except bitters to a mixing glass with ice
2. Stir 20 seconds and strain into a rocks glass filled with ice
3. Dash bitters on top to layer
ba-absinthe-old-fashioned.description: Doug Petry of Louisville’s Rye restaurant devised this absinthe-based old fashioned. It reads quite sweet but it rounds out nicely into a surprisingly delicious cocktail.

ba-adonis.method_text: Stir all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ba-adonis.description: The cocktail was created in honor of the 1884 musical Adonis after the show reached the milestone of more than 500 shows on Broadway.

ba-affinity.method_text:
1. Stir all of the ingredients with ice to chill
2. Strain into a chilled glass
ba-affinity.description: This off-the-radar classic cocktail was originally made with equal measures of Scotch whisky, dry vermouth, and sweet vermouth. At Bramble in Edinburgh, co-owner Jason Scott has developed, well, an affinity for the Affinity, brushing up the original recipe by using a Highland single malt (Glenmorangie 10 year old) and swapping in Byrrh Grand Quinquina for the sweet vermouth. The crowning touch? Bramble ages its mixture in barrels; they originally used small casks custom-made for the cocktails by Glenmorangie and are currently using 50-liter barrels that previously held oloroso sherry, aging the cocktail for between three and nine months and using a solera system for consistency. Until you can get to Edinburgh to try one of Bramble’s barrel-aged Affinity cocktails in person, here’s the base recipe, which should give you a delicious taste of the possibilities.

ba-after-all-imperial.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients, except sparkling wine, in a shaker and shake.
2. Strain into a collins glass or flute and top with sparkling wine.
3. Garnish with mint or rosemary
ba-after-all-imperial.description: A fruity spin on a light, bubbly classic
ba-after-all-imperial.garnish: Sprig mint or rosemary for garnish

ba-airmail.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients except for the champagne in a mixer and shake for ten seconds
2. Strain into a flute and top with champagne
ba-airmail.description: An endlessly drinkable sparkler of debated origin

ba-alabazam.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients with ice and shake
2. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass, serve up
ba-alabazam.description: One of the oldest sours, this drink also uses an enormous portion of Angostura bitters

ba-alaska.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients with ice in a mixing glass and stir at length, until the sides of the glass are frosty
2. Strain into a cocktail glass and serve up
ba-alaska.description: One of the great Chartreuse cocktails and a fundamental three-ingredient recipe

ba-amalfi-frappe.method_text:
1. Combine the ingredients in a glass, then add shaved ice and stir briefly to incorporate.
2. Top with more shaved ice and garnish.
ba-amalfi-frappe.description: For this frappe, Little Rituals owner Ross Simon wanted to capture the flavors of the Amalfi Coast. "Amalfi is famous for its citrus and citrus infusions, so he used our house limoncello (a recipe from sister bar Bitter & Twisted Cocktail Parlor) and wanted to make it frappe style," says bar director Aaron Defeo. "We punched the drink up with a healthy dose of Strega, an Italian liqueur with notes of saffron, mint, fennel. All those flavors love fresh lemon, and we’ve got plenty of that in there. It’s a simple but flavorful drink that keeps getting better the longer it sits."

ba-amaretto-sour-jeffrey-morgenthaler.method_text:
1. Combine ingredients in a cocktail shaker and shake without ice or (even better) use an immersion blender to combine and froth.
2. Shake well with cracked ice.
3. Strain over fresh ice in an old fashioned glass
ba-amaretto-sour-jeffrey-morgenthaler.description:
There are two things that impede all other Amaretto Sours from challenging mine. First off, the obvious: they’re too sweet. One does not simply use an everyday sour recipe to make a world-class Amaretto Sour, it must be adjusted for this particular liqueur.

Second, and this is a big one: amaretto isn’t strong enough on its own to stand up to a bunch of other ingredients. It’s weak. It needs help. And for this, I enlist the assistance of an old friend. One that knows amaretto’s strengths and weaknesses. Or, mainly, its weaknesses. One that works with amaretto, to complete it like Jerry Maguire completes Rene Zellwiger’s character, whatever her name was. And that, my friends, is cask-proof bourbon.
ba-amaretto-sour-jeffrey-morgenthaler.garnish: Garnish with lemon peel and brandied cherries.

ba-amaro-highball.method_text:
1. Add all of the ingredients, except the soda water, to a shaker filled with ice.
2. Shake and then strain into an ice-filled glass.
3. Top with the soda.
ba-amaro-highball.description: Julep Houston bartender David Kubiak created this amaro highball to highlight Amaro Montenegro and serve as an intro to mezcal.

ba-amen-corner.method_text:
1. Gently muddle the mint in a mixing tin.
2. Combine remaining ingredients in the mixing tin and shake with ice.
3. Strain into a chilled coupe.
4. Garnish with brandied cherries.
ba-amen-corner.description: Created by PDT alum Nick Brown, the bourbon-based cocktail recipe is a riff on the classic Paper Plane without the lemon juice.

ba-amoxicillin.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients, except the peated Scotch, in a mixing tin and shake with ice.
2. Strain into a rocks glass over ice.
3. Finish with six sprays of peated Scotch from an atomizer.
4. Garnish with a lemon wheel.
ba-amoxicillin.description: Unlike the classic Penicillin, which calls for ¾ ounce honey-ginger syrup, this cocktail recipe uses yellow Chartreuse for honeyed sweetness.

ba-ancho-problem.method_text:
1. Shake all ingredients with ice.
2. Strain into chilled cocktail glass.
ba-ancho-problem.description: In response to the request for "something spicy, with tequila," Ezra Star whips up this chile- and blanco tequila-spiked cocktail recipe.

ba-andalusian-buck.method_text:
1. Combine gin, sherry, lime juice, and Demerara syrup in a cocktail shaker with ice.
2. Shake until cold.
3. I like to add the ginger beer directly to the shaker, then pour slowly over fresh ice in a chilled Collins glass.
ba-andalusian-buck.description: This drink is great because it doesn’t go too far any any direction. It’s not too sweet, there’s only a teaspoon of sugar in the whole thing. It’s not too sour, there’a barely half a lime’s worth of juice. And it’s not too strong, it only calls for an ounce of gin. And between the ginger beer and the Amontillado sherry, it’s absolutely bursting with flavor. In sort, it’s refreshing and crushable, but still interesting, which was exactly the type of drink we specialized in at Clyde Common.

ba-angie.method_text:
1. Add all of the ingredients to a shaker with ice. Shake to chill, then strain into the glass. Garnish.
Passion Fruit SyrupCombine 1 cup of passion fruit purée and 1 cup of superfine sugar in a pot and boil. Allow to cool, then strain. Will keep in the refrigerator for 2 weeks.
ba-angie.description: During a visit to Panama in 2017, Bratislav Glisic, head bartender and co-founder of Dear Strangers in New York, had his first taste of maracujá, aka passion fruit. Enamored by its appearance and flavor, he decided to create a tropical cocktail to showcase the fruit. Using the classic Pisco Sour as a template, Glisic balances the sweet tartness of passion fruit with gin, elderflower, and lemon. The earthiness from a sprinkle of matcha powder rounds out the flavors.
ba-angie.garnish: Matcha powder and dehydrated lime wheel

ba-annas-revenge.method_text: 1. Add all of the ingredients to a shaker with ice. Shake and then strain into the glass. Garnish.
ba-annas-revenge.description: Since Brooklyn's Bar Camillo features a range of bitter-forward cocktails, head bartender Anna Wang sought to create a lighter and refreshing alternative at Suono, the hi-fi bar below the restaurant. "I wanted to make a cocktail that would introduce to our customers the more delicate floral notes often found in some of the lighter Italian amari and digestivi, like Montenegro and Strega," she says. And determined to keep the recipe simple, there's no fussy bar prep or homemade ingredients involved. But to keep the flavors balanced, Wang insists on using an agave-forward mezcal versus an "overly smokey one" so as not to overpower the amari's herbaceousness.

ba-apapacho-cafe.method_text:
1. Pour the first 4 ingredients into the glass and gently stir. Add the whipping cream to a shaker with an ice cube and shake very hard. Strain over the cocktail, then grate the nutmeg over the top.
2. Note: The bar mixes a bit of pinole with nutmeg (4:1) for the garnish, but nutmeg alone works fine if you don’t have pinole.
ba-apapacho-cafe.description: This twist on classic Irish coffee from Rosewood Mayakoba's Zapote Bar, one of the 50 Best Bars in North America, is just the thing for a chilly day. Apapacho, which translates to "a warm hug," combines hot coffee with bourbon and vermouth rosso and is topped with freshly whipped cream.

ba-apb-melrose-gin-tonic.method_text:
1. Add the first 4 ingredients to a shaker with ice. Shake until chilled, then strain into a glass over fresh ice. Add the tonic, top with pebble ice, then drizzle the blue Chareau on top. Garnish.
2. Blue ChareauAnd 1/8 tsp. of blue spirulina to 1/2 cup Chareau and whisk. Will keep in the refrigerator for 2 weeks.
ba-apb-melrose-gin-tonic.description: This mesmerizingly azure-topped gin and tonic from Los Angeles' APB (A Plant Bar) Melrose draws inspiration from the state of California. Drink creator Julian Cox selected the Golden State's Gray Whale gin for its Californian ingredients, such as citrus and sea kelp. But he says that a botanical forward new Western gin can also be used in its place. "The cocktail takes you on a journey of floral and citrus flavors," Cox says. "It starts with a light and effervescent quality that lingers through the finish."

ba-apero-spritz.method_text:
1. Add first four ingredients to a shaker tin with ice and short shake.
2. Double strain into a wine glass over cracked clear ice and top with prosecco.
3. Garnish with red currants if you have them, lemon wedge if you don’t

ba-aperol-spritz.method_text: Build all ingredients into a wine glass filled with ice. Stir gently.
ba-aperol-spritz.description: A Spritz is a Venetian wine-based cocktail, commonly served as an aperitif in Northeast Italy. It consists of prosecco, digestive bitters and soda water. The Spritz became widely popular outside of Italy around 2018 and Aperol Spritz was ranked as the world's ninth bestselling cocktail in 2019 by the website Drinks International.
ba-aperol-spritz.garnish: Garnish with a slice of orange.

ba-appetizer-a-litalienne.method_text:
1. Stir all of the ingredients with ice, then strain into a chilled glass. Express the twists over the finished cocktail, and use as a garnish.
2. Tip Schmidt didn’t specify a garnish for the drink in his 1892 book, but Yarm says a lemon twist “would smooth out the fernet’s aggression, and an orange twist to sweeten things would be nice, too.
ba-appetizer-a-litalienne.description:
It could be argued that the difference between a forgotten cocktail and a beloved classic is simply the size of the audience. The Appetizer à l’Italienne appeared in William Schmidt’s The Flowing Bowl in 1892, then largely disappeared. (A similar recipe, for the absinthe-free Bonsoni Cocktail, appeared in Hugo Ensslin’s Recipes for Mixed Drinks in 1917.) With its aggressive match of sweet vermouth and Fernet-Branca accented with absinthe, the cocktail’s character is rooted in the late 19th century, and out of place in the 20th.

But the cocktail renaissance brought both a taste for bold, bitter combinations, and an interest in historical spelunking. Boston bartender Frederic Yarm recalls being served the Appetizer à l’Italienne in 2009 at the cocktail bar Drink, years before he joined the team (he left the bar in November). Yarm says the recipe is still included in Drink’s cocktail manual, and its simple formula fills a certain historical niche. “It’s a recipe I wouldn’t want to modify, since it is what it is and a showing of what some bartenders were doing 130 years ago,” Yarm says. 

To balance the brawn of fernet and absinthe, Yarm says it’s important to use a richer style of vermouth, such as Carpano Antica Formula or a Vermouth di Torino. And don’t skip the simple syrup: “The sugar’s important here to convert fernet from a digestif to an aperitif, as suggested by the drink’s name,” Yarm says. “The drier version pushes the digestive system to wrap up eating."

ba-apple-amaretto-sour.description: Autumn variation of Amaretto Sour by Anders
ba-apple-amaretto-sour.garnish: Express lemon oils, add cocktail cherry

ba-apple-kickin.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a rocks glass with a large format ice cube
2. Stir for 20 seconds
ba-apple-kickin.description: A bold, lightly bitter Old Fashioned variant whose flavor profile is an intriguing blend of fresh apple alongside spiced sugarcane.

ba-apples-all-the-way-down.method_text:
1. Add syrup, lemon, and brandy to a highball glass filled with ice
2. Top with cider and stir
3. Slap a sprig of rosemary to release its oils and garnish
ba-apples-all-the-way-down.description: A dash of bitters and fresh rosemary balance the sweetness of this bright highball that's brimming with fall fruit flavor.

ba-apricot-and-coffee-highball.method_text:
1. Add the first 4 ingredients to the ice-filled glass and stir to combine.
2. Top with tonic water, then garnish.
ba-apricot-and-coffee-highball.description: Apricot and coffee might not seem like an obvious flavor duo, but at Too Soon in Portland, Oregon, the idea to combine them in a cocktail came about from "wanting to explore contrast in a really approachable format," says owner/operator Nick Flower. The combination with a hint of peated smoke from the Islay scotch gives compelling depth to a bright and bubbly highball. "We’ve always loved coffee and tonic together. The subtle, crisp bitterness keeps it from reading too rich," adds Flower.

ba-archangel.method_text:
1. In a mixing glass, bruise cucumber slices with a muddler.
2. Add gin, Aperol, ice and stir until chilled.
3. Strain into a chilled coupe or cocktail glass.
4. Garnish with a lemon peel.
ba-archangel.description: A play on a Pink Gin, the Archangel cocktail recipe combines the aromatic subtlety of cucumbers, the orange of Aperol and the strength of gin.

ba-army-navy.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice and shake until chilled.
2. Strain into a chilled coupe or cocktail glass.
ba-army-navy.description: The Army & Navy is a tropical gin cocktail recipe made with gin, lemon juice, orgeat and Angostura bitters.

ba-arrowhead-limited.method_text:
1. Add Campari, mezcal and Carpano Antica to a high ball glass.
2. Add ice, and top with IPA.
3. Garnish with grapefruit slices.
ba-arrowhead-limited.description: Ever a lover of combining beer with bitters, Damon Boelte tops this "mezcal Negroni" cocktail recipe with IPA.

ba-arsenic-and-old-lace.method_text:
1. Using an atomizer, spritz a chilled coupe glass with absinthe.
2. Combine all other ingredients in a mixing glass and stir with ice.
3. Strain into prepared glass.
4. Express a lemon twist over the drink, then use as garnish.
ba-arsenic-and-old-lace.description: The Arsenic and Old Lace is a Martini cocktail recipe made with gin, absinthe, dry vermouth, crème de violette and Angostura bitters.

ba-art-of-choke.method_text:
1. Muddle mint and syrup in a mixing glass
2. Add remaining with ice and stir for 20 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled rocks glass with fresh ice
ba-art-of-choke.description: A drink that broke all the rules when Kyle Davidson first conjured it in 2008. Now it's a modern classic. What's interesting is opting for a split base where one half is an overproof amaro instead of a spirit. Also wild - this is a stirred cocktail!

ba-artichoke-hold.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker.
2. Add a small amount of ice and shake lightly.
3. Strain over crushed ice into a rocks glass.
4. Top with more crushed ice.
ba-artichoke-hold.description: The warm funk of Smith & Cross rum creates a heavy base for the bittersweet co-mingling of amaro and elderflower in this cocktail recipe.

ba-as-kingston-negroni.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice and stir until chilled.
2. Taste occasionally to ensure the coffee bean flavor has infused the drink.
3. Strain into a rocks glass over a large ice cube.
4. Garnish with a half orange wheel and lime twist.
ba-as-kingston-negroni.description: A Kingston Negroni cocktail recipe that stirs the classic mix of rum, Campari and sweet vermouth with oloroso sherry and coffee beans.

ba-aspen-crud.method_text:
1. Add bourbon and ice cream to a blender and blitz until creamy.
2. Pour into a pint glass or Mason jar and garnish with cherries, if using. Serve with a straw.
ba-aspen-crud.description: Invented at Hotel Jerome during Prohibition, the Aspen Crud cocktail is a symbol of the ski town's pre-glitz history and an enduring staple.

ba-assunta.method_text: 1. Add the ingredients, except the ginger beer, to a shaker with ice and shake vigorously. Pour into a highball filled with crushed ice and top with ginger beer, then garnish.
ba-assunta.description: Since every cocktail at Saint Theo's is a nod to an Italian name, ingredient, or garnish, beverage director Simon Sebbah transformed the Moscow Mule into an Italian Mule by sweetening it with amaretto.

ba-autoretrato.method_text:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a cocktail shaker.
2. Dry shake to emulsify the egg whites.
3. Add ice and shake until chilled.
4. Double strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
5. Garnish with a half of passion fruit, mint leaf and a dried clover blossom.
ba-autoretrato.description: Autoretrato is a tropical riff on the modern classic Amaretto Sour, reinvented for a different audience. The spirit base is pisco, which offers distinct grape notes, subtle floral and fruity flavors that pair well with the sweet, nutty amaretto. Passion fruit pulp gives the drink a tiki-like direction with a balanced sweet-tart fruitiness, while agave nectar and lemon juice add a floral tartness. Egg whites provide a foamy, decadent texture. It is a deliciously complex and fruity cocktail, suitable for garden parties and summer gatherings.
ba-autoretrato.garnish: Mint leaf, dried clover blossom, half of passion fruit

ba-avenue-scotch.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 10 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled Nick & Nora glass
ba-avenue-scotch.description: From frigid Iceland comes this tropical sour. Created by Jónmundur Þorsteinsson.

ba-baby-turtle.method_text:
1. Add all of the ingredients to a shaker and dry-shake (without ice) to combine.
2. Add ice to the shaker and shake until chilled.
3. Double-strain into a double Old-Fashioned glass over ice.
ba-baby-turtle.description: A tequila cocktail recipe that combines reposado tequila, Campari, grapefruit and lime juice, cinnamon syrup and saline.

ba-backlash-tonic.method_text: 1. Combine all of the ingredients in a glass with a large ice cube and briefly stir to combine, and garnish.
ba-backlash-tonic.description: This simple aperitivo cocktail offers layers of flavor from Melbourne's Pendant Public Bar.

ba-backsliding-presbyterian.method_text: Shake all ingredients (except club soda) with ice and strain into an ice-filled glass. Top with club soda and garnish.
ba-backsliding-presbyterian.description: Tall and bursting with bittersweet orange and ginger flavors, this whiskey highball proves that aged spirits aren’t just for winter sipping.

ingredients.name: Overproof Rum
ingredients.note: preferably Rum-Bar Overproof White Jamaican Rum

ba-bahama-mama.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a mixing tin. Add 5 ice cubes and shake for 5 seconds.
2. Strain into a Hurricane glass filled with crushed ice.
3. Garnish with tropical fruit.
ba-bahama-mama.description: Tiki master Paul McGee’s recalibrated version of this classic cocktail recipe involves dialing down the proportions and sweetness.

ingredients.name: Light Rum
ingredients.note: such as Don Q Cristal or El Dorado 3-year

ba-baltimore-southside.method_text:
1. Combine the rum, lemon juice, simple syrup and mint in a shaker with ice.
2. Shake until chilled.
3. Strain into a double rocks glass over 1.25-inch ice cubes.
4. Top with about 1 1/2 ounces of club soda.
5. Garnish with mint and a lemon wheel.
ba-baltimore-southside.description: A Southside that honors the legacy of Baltimore's Black bartenders.
ba-baltimore-southside.garnish: mint bouquet, lemon wheel or dehydrated lemon wheel

ba-banana-daiquiri.method_text:
1. Put all of the ingredients into a blender and blend until smooth.
2. Pour into the chilled glass, and garnish.
ba-banana-daiquiri.description: Popular at tropical bars and often sold in prefabricated mixes, blended versions of the classic Daiquiri rarely garner the same respect as their three-ingredient forebears. It’s a shame because a properly made Banana Daiquiri is bright and balanced. Credit for the creation is frequently given to Harry K. Yee, the legendary bartender who also invented the Blue Hawaii cocktail and pioneered the use of orchid and paper umbrella garnishes during his 30-year tenure at Waikiki’s Hawaiian Village Hotel. At Palomar, a Cuba-inspired cocktail bar in Portland, Oregon, owner Ricky Gomez serves a Banana Daiquiri recipe made with aged rum, tart lime, and a carefully calibrated combination of banana liqueur and fresh bananas. “When you use only bananas, it ends up just tasting like a smoothie with rum. We wanted it to still be a cocktail,” says Gomez. Those fresh bananas are treated with care. Palomar keeps the chunked fruit at 17 degrees Fahrenheit, whereas most household freezers are set to 0 degrees Fahrenheit, so they blend evenly and require less ice to reach frothy perfection. To mimic this at home, let fully frozen pieces of fruit sit at room temperature for approximately 10 minutes on the kitchen counter, then pop everything into a blender and set sail.
ba-banana-daiquiri.garnish: Three pieces of banana-shaped hard candy (optional)

ba-barbacoa.method_text:
1. In a cocktail shaker, combine all the ingredients and muddle them together.
2. Add ice and shake until chilled.
3. Pour into a double Old-Fashioned glass.
4. Garnish with a piece of beef jerky.
ba-barbacoa.description: The Barbacoa is a mezcal cocktail recipe that muddles fresh ginger syrup and lemon juice with bell peppers and Fresno chile.

ba-barmuda-triangle.method_text:
1. Shake with pebble ice.
2. Strain into a cocktail glass.
3. Garnish.

ba-basil-julep.method_text:
1. Muddle 2-3 basil leaves with gum syrup in a julep cup
2. Fill with crushed ice and add whiskey
3. Stir until cold and frosty, then top with more crushed ice
ba-basil-julep.description: Pick a high-character Irish Whiskey - something with rich, oily spice notes to pull down the basil's volatile peppery aroma.

ba-batanga.method_text:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a highball glass with ice.
2. Stir to combine.
ba-batanga.description: First created at a bar called La Capilla in the town of Tequila by Don Javier Delgado Corona in the 1960s, the Batanga is a favorite among fans of agave spirits. At Ghost Donkey (our 2020 Cocktail Bar of the Year) the classic combo of tequila, lime and cola gets an added layer of bittersweetness courtesy of a Mexican Fernet. You can experiment with whatever Fernet you have on hand, but Ignacio "Nacho" Jimenez says Fernet-Vallet will bring a deeper bark-like dryness to the mix.

ba-bay-ridge.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients except garnish in a mixing glass filled with ice.
2. Stir for 15–20 seconds until well chilled.
3. Strain into chilled coupe or Nick & Nora glass, and garnish with an orange twist.
ba-bay-ridge.description: The Bay Ridge, which originated at Brooklyn cocktail lounge Clover Club around 2014, represents a long line of New York-themed cocktails based on the Manhattan. Here's how it differs, and why it matters.

ba-bebbo.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker.
2. Add ice and shake until well-chilled.
3. Strain into a chilled coupe and garnish with a stripe of Angostura bitters.
ba-bebbo.description: The Bebbo is a cocktail recipe that riffs on the classic Bee’s Knees. The gin drink is made with lemon and orange juices plus honey syrup.

ba-bee-sting.method_text:
1. Add the Bärenjäger, Laphroaig, Fernet-Branca, egg white and tangerine juice into a shaker and vigorously dry-shake (without ice).
2. Fill with ice and shake again until well-chilled.
3. Double-strain into an Old Fashioned glass filled with fresh ice.
4. Top with the bitters.
ba-bee-sting.description: Scotch, honey and herbal liqueurs come together in this unconventional drink from bartender Jonathan Pogash.

ba-beet-it.method_text:
1. Pour all of the ingredients into a shaker.
2. Add ice, give it a good shake and strain.
3. Serve up, into a coupe or martini glass.
4. Top with drops of olive oil.

**Note:** No prebottled beet juice will live up to freshly juiced beets. If you don't have your own juicer at home, the best option is to swing by your local fresh juice shop and have them make you a fresh batch. A 16-oz. to-go cup will make 16 cocktails. Natural grocery stores carry decent bottled beet juice, but they generally add acid in the form of lemon juice and citric acid as a preservative, in which case you can pull back on the amount of lime juice to keep the cocktail balanced.
ba-beet-it.description: According to Chris D'Apice, beverage director of San Diego's Books & Records, this mezcal beet cocktail drinks like an earthy, vegetal Margarita. Garnishing the cocktail with drops of olive oil enhances its savory character while also giving it a velvety mouthfeel.

ba-belleville.method_text:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice and expressed lemon peel. Stir to chill, then strain over a large ice cube in the glass. Garnish with a lemon peel.
2. Note“This cocktail calls for a very under-utilized technique called the ‘Royal Stir’ where we incorporate a lemon peel in the mixing glass to gently add brightness and texture during the stir—but not getting in the way of the aromatics of the final cocktail via an expression. We encourage home bartenders to experiment with this approach if they want to highlight the high quality of the spirits that are being used rather than the citrus garnish.”—Allison Lovelace
ba-belleville.description: At Atlanta bistro Little Sparrow, the cocktails skew classic with French accents. This Manhattan-inspired cocktail balances bourbon with crème de cassis, sweet vermouth, and a French bitter for an elegant and layered sipper.

ba-bentons-old-fashioned.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass.
2. Add ice and stir until chilled.
3. Strain into a rocks glass over ice (preferably a large cube).
4. Garnish with an orange peel.
ba-bentons-old-fashioned.description: The Benton’s Old-Fashioned cocktail recipe is the drink that introduced the concept of “fat-washing” spirits to the cocktail world.

ba-beton.method_text:
1. Add ingredients to a highball glass with ice.
2. Garnish with a lemon slice.
ba-beton.description: The Beton is a Czech cocktail starring Becherovka, an herbal liqueur, and tonic water, that is sometimes compared to a Gin and Tonic.

ba-betty-carter.method_text:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a cocktail shaker.
2. Add ice and shake until chilled.
3. Double strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
ba-betty-carter.description:
Most whiskey and bourbon-based cocktails are synonymous with the cold time of the year, when one turns to the warming qualities of these spirits. Betty Carter, on the other hand, hits a nice middle ground, possessing enough refreshing qualities making it very suitable for the warm periods as well.

Base of the cocktail is bourbon with strong notes of oak, vanilla and caramel. It is then paired with sweet profile of PX sherry and its signature intense fruity notes like figs and dates, giving the cocktail a little lightness. This bright impression is then further reinforced by a healthy does of tart lemon juice, changing the overall flavour profile closer to a sour cocktail style. Touch of amaro Nonino, gives the cocktail a further complexity with delicate sweet orange notes balanced by the bitterness of gentian root and quinine.

Betty Carter, is a cocktail with a pretty straight forward build, just requiring to source a somewhat harder to get amaro, but once you have it you are good to go. Simple to make, delicious and remarkably refreshing. Suitable to drink all year round, although for the winter period, I would probably add a little bit of simple syrup to reign in the tartness, or look for a slightly sweeter and bolder PX Sherry.
ba-betty-carter.garnish: Garnish with an orange twist and a sprig of mint.

ba-betty-is-back.method_text: 1. Combine all of the ingredients, except the Champagne, in a mixing glass filled with ice and stir until well chilled. Strain into a flute and gently pour in the Champagne. Garnish.
ba-betty-is-back.description: Named for the Connaught Bar's head bartender during the 1940s, this sparkler was the first cocktail on the famed bar's menu when it reopened in 2008. "Betty is Back is a dry, bubbly sip with delicate floral and citrus notes from a complex blend of Aperol ... and elderflower liqueurs and fresh lemon juice," writes Ago Perrone in his book, The Connaught Bar: Recipes and Iconic Creations, "while the Champagne raises a toast to this memorable wartime bartender and her customers, who kept returning to this iconic spot for more."

ba-beuser-angus-special.method_text:
1. Combine the first five ingredients in a cocktail shaker and shake hard with ice.
2. Strain into a rocks glass filled with ice.
3. Top with orange flower water.
ba-beuser-angus-special.description: Chartreuse sour from Berlin, the Beuser & Angus Special takes inspiration from the Last Word and the Ramos Gin Fizz. Created in 2007 by Gonçalo de Sousa Monteiro for fellow bartenders Bastian Heuser and Angus Winchester, the drink has gone on to become a modern classic.

ba-bijou.method_text: Stir in mixing glass with ice and strain
ba-bijou.description: This cocktail was invented by Harry Johnson, "the father of professional bartending", who called it bijou because it combined the colors of three jewels: gin for diamond, vermouth for ruby, and chartreuse for emerald.

ba-bijou-blanc.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
2. Stir until chilled.
3. Strain into a rocks glass over ice.
4. Garnish with a lemon peel “flag.”
ba-bijou-blanc.description: A modern take on the Bijou, this cocktail recipe puts a fresh spin on the classic Chartreuse cocktail, similar to a White Negroni.

ba-bitter-giuseppe.method_text:
1. Stir all the ingredients together in a mixing glass with ice until chilled.
2. Strain into a rocks glass over a single large ice cube and garnish.
ba-bitter-giuseppe.description: First featured on an early menu at the Violet Hour in Chicago, Stephen Cole's Bitter Giuseppe cocktail has become a modern classic over the years, with iterations popping up on menus at places like Cure in New Orleans, Elske and Ludlow Liquors in Chicago.

ba-bitter-mai-tai.method_text:
1. Combine all the ingredients in a cocktail shaker. Add ice and shake until chilled, about 10 seconds.
2. Strain into a large rocks glass over crushed ice.
3. Garnish with mint sprig.


 ## Editors note:

### Orgeat:

300 grams raw almonds (about 3 1⁄2 cups/ 1⁄2 pound)

Water, as needed

Sugar



Put the almonds in a bowl and add water to cover. Set aside tosoak overnight. Drain the water, then weigh the almonds. Transferthem to a blender and slowly add an equal weight of fresh waterwhile the blender is running on slow, for about 1 minute. Increaseto high speed, until the mixture is opaque. Strain through a nutmilk bag or a fine- mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth. Weigh thestrained milk. Transfer to a medium saucepan and add an equalweight of sugar. Heat over medium, stirring, until the sugar hasdissolved. Remove from the heat and let cool. Store in an airtightcontainer in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.
ba-bitter-mai-tai.description: Perhaps the most riffed-upon cocktail in the tiki canon, the Mai Tai cocktail recipe serves as the inspiration for this bitter spin.

ba-black-manhattan.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice and stir until chilled.
2. Strain into a chilled coupe.
3. Garnish with a cherry.
ba-black-manhattan.description: Amaro Averna stands in for sweet vermouth in this Manhattan-inspired modern classic cocktail recipe from Todd Smith.

ba-black-walnut-old-fashioned.method_text: Combine ingredients in a mixing glass with ice. Stir until chilled. Strain into an Old Fashioned glass with fresh ice.
ba-black-walnut-old-fashioned.description: If you are after an Old Fashioned riff with a warming complexity then a Walnut Old Fashioned should hit the spot. So further spike your Bourbon & Orange Bitters with a little Walnut Liqueur for a drink that glides effortlessly down your throat.

ba-blackberry-whiskey-smash.method_text:
1. Muddle berries, mint, and syrup in a mixing tin 
2. Add lemon juice, whiskey and ice 
3. Shake until chilled
4. Double strain over crushed ice into a rocks glass
ba-blackberry-whiskey-smash.description: Fruit-forward without being too sweet. A perfect spring and early summer drink.

ba-blackthorn.method_text: 1. Stir all of the ingredients with ice, then strain into a glass filled with fresh ice, and garnish.
ba-blackthorn.description: With roots dating back to 19th-century New Orleans, the Blackthorn cocktail is one of the few classics to highlight Irish whiskey. Here's how they make it at Lazy Bird in Chicago.

ba-blinker.method_text:
1. Combine all the ingredients except the grapefruit twist in a cocktail shaker filled with ice and shake until chilled, about 15 seconds.
2. Strain into a chilled coupe.
3. Twist a piece of grapefruit zest over the drink and drop into the glass.
ba-blinker.description: Calling on a full ounce of grenadine to complement the grapefruit juice and rye base, this cocktail recipe is potent but refreshing.

ba-blood-and-sand.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients with ice and shake
2. Strain into a coupe
3. Flame orange peel and garnish
ba-blood-and-sand.description: An exceptionally smooth classic with an optional smoky finish

ba-blood-moon.method_text: 1. Build in a wine glass over ice and garnish with a orange half-moon
ba-blood-moon.description: The Blood Moon cocktail recipe is just one example of Joe Campanale's ode to aperitivo, on the menu at Alta Linea.

ba-bloody-caesar.method_text:
1. Coat the rim of a tall glass with celery salt, fill with ice and set aside.
2. Add the vodka, Clamato juice, Worcestershire sauce, Tabasco and horseradish into a mixing glass with ice.
3. Pour back and forth into another mixing glass a few times to combine.
4. Strain into the prepared glass.
5. Garnish with a celery stalk, cucumber spear and lime wedge.
ba-bloody-caesar.description: The Bloody Caesar is a clam-juice-spiked riff on the Bloody Mary. And it’s the national cocktail of Canada.

ba-bloom-no-5.method_text:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a shaker with ice and shake vigorously.
2. Strain into a chilled coupe.
3. Express a lemon peel and use as a garnish.
ba-bloom-no-5.description: "The goal behind the Bloom No. 5 was to weave floral, springtime flavors into a classic Margarita template," says Shelby Abell, bartender at Nashville's Martha My Dear. To do this she combines Suze and elderflower liqueur, which balance one another and create a complex, bittersweet profile. Meanwhile, ginger and lemon brighten up the drink "to nail the 'springtime in a glass' vibe," Abell adds.

ba-blue-hawaii.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a shaker tin.
2. Flash-blend for 4 to 5 seconds with 4 ounces of crushed ice.
3. Pour into a hurricane glass over 8 ounces of crushed ice.
4. Garnish with sliced pineapple, pineapple fronds and an orchid.
ba-blue-hawaii.description: Adapted from a recipe created in 1957 by Harry K. Yee at Henry Kaiser's Hawaiian Village Hotel (latterly the Hilton) in Waikiki, Oahu, Hawaii. The drink, created at the behest of Bols to aid sales of their blue curaçao, is named after the hit song from the 1937 Bing Crosby film, Waikiki Wedding, and not after what is generously described as a "musical-comedy" Elvis Presley 1961 film of the same name. That said, the Elvis film probably contributed to this cocktail's popularity.

ba-bluebird-eggnog.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a shaker and dry-shake vigorously.
2. Add ice, and quickly hard-shake.
3. Double-strain into a rocks glass with light ice.
4. To garnish, place a white chocolate eggshell on top of the cocktail.


 ## Editors note:

### White Chocolate Eggshell

Temper high-quality white chocolate. While the chocolate is heating, blow up water balloons to roughly the size of an extra-large egg, and assemble a cold water bath. 

When the white chocolate is tempered, dip the balloon halfway and allow the chocolate to drip off, then place directly into the cold water to set.

Once the chocolate has set, pop the balloon with a paring knife or scissors, and peel it away from the chocolate shell. Chocolate eggs may be stored in the freezer until ready to use.
ba-bluebird-eggnog.description: This eggnog cocktail recipe from Baltimore bar The Bluebird combines cream, rum, apple brandy, an egg and simple syrup.

ba-bon-soiree.method_text:
1. Rim a chilled glass with tajin.
2. Combine the ingredients in a shaker with ice.
3. Shake to chill, then strain into the prepared glass.
ba-bon-soiree.description: This cocktail from Hailey Knight and Casey Knight (no relation) of Charleston's Félix Cocktails et Cuisine takes the spicy Margarita for an extra-savory spin. Saline lends a saltiness, while Lillet Blanc rounds out the edges of the fresh lime juice. Meanwhile, Knight recommends using your favorite hot sauce to spice it up. "The key is to use a vinegar-based hot sauce to complement the cocktail’s flavors rather than compete with them," she says. "I’m partial to Slap Ya Mama hot sauce."

ingredients.name: Sparkling wine
ingredients.note: such as Prosecco, Cava, or Champagne

ba-boothby.method_text: 1. In an ice-filled mixing glass, combine the first four ingredients and stir to chill. Strain into a chilled coupe and top with sparkling wine. Garnish with the skewered cherry.
ba-boothby.description: Proof that tinkering with classic cocktails is an evergreen endeavor, the Boothby is a pre-Prohibition Manhattan variant with an effervescent crown. Bartender, author, and erstwhile California State Assemblyman William T. Boothby is believed to have created the drink while working at San Francisco’s Palace Hotel around the turn of the 20th century. “Boothby was an interesting character,” says H. Joseph Ehrmann, proprietor of Elixir in San Francisco, California, where the Boothby has long been a menu staple. “He started out as a performer and didn’t start bartending until around 1890.” His namesake cocktail has a flair for the dramatic, too. The spirit-forward drink combines whiskey, sweet vermouth, and two types of bitters with a Champagne float. “You add bubbles to anything and make it better,” says Ehrmann, who jokes that he’s pleased that Boothby didn’t end up naming the drink a Manhattan Royale. When making a Boothby, Ehrmann prefers to use 90- to 100-proof rye and dry sparkling wine. “I like the complexity, spice, and punch that a bonded rye brings to the table, and the brut sparkling keeps the drink at the right balance while adding the necessary texture,” he says. Boozy and bubbly, it’s a drink for the ages.

ba-boozy-shakerato.method_text: 1. Combine the simple syrup, espresso and your choice of either limoncello, sambuca, or amaretto in shaker and fill with ice. Shake vigorously to create a fully aerated, fluffy drink. Strain into an after-dinner glass.
ba-boozy-shakerato.description: Perfect for an after dinner pick-me-up or a morning wake-up call, this boozy shakerato recipe is as versatile as it is delicious. Limoncello not your thing? Sub in 1/2 oz. sambuca or 1/2 oz. amaretto for a different spin.

ba-bourbon-lift.method_text:
1. Add the bourbon, coffee liqueur, heavy cream and orgeat into a shaker and vigorously dry-shake (without ice) for 10 seconds. Add ice and shake again until well-chilled.
2. Strain into a Collins glass.
3. Fill with the club soda, pouring from about 6 inches above the glass.
4. Wait a few seconds and then add another splash of soda. This will lift the foam above the top of the glass.
5. Serve with a straw.
ba-bourbon-lift.description: The cocktail equivalent of a New York egg cream, this rich and fizzy bourbon drink is absolutely delicious.

ba-bourbon-renewal.method_text:
1. Shake ingredients with ice until cold.
2. Strain over fresh ice into an old-fashioned glass.
3. Garnish with a lemon wedge, or if in season, fresh currants.
ba-bourbon-renewal.description:
This one was named after a band that my business partner, Tony Figoli was in a long time ago. I thought the name was absolutely brilliant, so I decided to do up a drink to commemorate the band – and my favorite spirit at the time.

I think the creme de cassis really works well with the sour component of this drink, and who can beat American whiskey on a warm spring evening?
ba-bourbon-renewal.garnish: Garnish with a lemon wedge, or if in season, fresh currants

ba-bourbon-stone-sour.method_text:
1. Combine bourbon, fresh orange juice, fresh lemon juice, and simple syrup in a cocktail shaker.
2. Add ice and shake until chilled.
3. Strain into a cocktail glass over fresh ice.
ba-bourbon-stone-sour.description: A refreshing bourbon cocktail designed for summer, combining citrus fruitiness with the spirit's notes of oak, vanilla, and caramel.
ba-bourbon-stone-sour.garnish: Orange slice, mint sprig, cocktail cherry

ba-brainstorm.method_text:
1. Stir all of the ingredients with ice, then strain into a chilled glass.
2. Twist an orange peel over the cocktail and use as garnish.
ba-brainstorm.description: This classic Irish whiskey cocktail from Hugo Ensslin’s 1917 Recipes for Mixed Drinks has been adapted for contemporary use, with the French vermouth and honeyed herbal liqueur Bénédictine given greater billing in the glass.

ba-brasserie-special.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 20 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled coupe
ba-brasserie-special.description: Bring a bottle of whiskey to the island with this passionfruit-based sour. From the Café Royal Cocktail Book, the Brasserie Special showcases how versatile passion fruit syrup is, and how whiskey can go tiki!

ba-breakfast-margarita.method_text:
1. Add all of the ingredients to a shaker with ice and shake to chill.
2. Fine strain into a glass over fresh ice.
3. Garnish.
ba-breakfast-margarita.description: There are several takes on the Breakfast Margarita, a Marg inspired by Salvatore Calabrese's Breakfast Martini. But at Superbueno, Nacho Jimenez mixes the modern classic with the Cadillac Margarita, using Grand Marnier instead of Cointreau. The bar makes its own mole orange marmalade, but Jimenez says a "good orange marmalade like Bonne Maman" seasoned with mole spices can be swapped in its place. "The Grand Marnier adds some complexity to this drink, and the mole orange marmalade adds more depth and flavor from the spices and chiles," he says.

ba-breakfast-martini.method_text:
1. Stir the marmalade with the lemon juice at the bottom of a cocktail shaker until it dissolves.
2. Add the gin and Curaçao. Shake with ice. Fine strain into a chilled cocktail coupe.
3. Shred some orange peel on the top of the drink as a garnish.
ba-breakfast-martini.description: This cocktail recipe is one of the earliest—and still the most famous—examples of jam as an ingredient in a cocktail revival era.

ba-bright-orchard-gin-and-tonic.method_text:
1. Fill a highball glass with ice.
2. Pour in the gin, apple juice, and lemon juice.
3. Top with light tonic water.
4. Stir once to integrate.
5. Garnish with an apple slice and rosemary sprig.
ba-bright-orchard-gin-and-tonic.description: A refreshing winter variation of the classic gin and tonic that combines orchard fruits, citrus, and juniper notes. Designed to be low in sugar and calories, this crisp beverage offers subtle digestive and mood-supporting qualities while delivering a clean, dry finish.

ba-brown-bomber.method_text: Stir all ingredients with ice and strain into chilled glass.
ba-brown-bomber.description: Similar to white negroni but built with whiskey

ba-brown-derby.method_text:
1. Add the ingredients into a shaker with ice and shake until well-chilled.

2. Fine-strain into a cocktail glass.

3. Express the oil from a grapefruit twist over the drink and drop the twist into the drink to garnish.
ba-brown-derby.description: The Brown Derby cocktail, a classic bourbon drink, was named for the famous Los Angeles diner and is both sweet and sour.

ba-bywater.method_text:
1. Stir all ingredients until chilled in a mixing glass filled with ice.
2. Strain into a coupe or a Nick & Nora glass.
3. Express an orange twist over the surface, then discard. Garnish with a cherry.
ba-bywater.description: The Bywater is a rum and Chartreuse cocktail recipe from New Orleans that riffs on the Brooklyn, itself a Manhattan riff.

ba-cable-car.method_text:
1. Start with rimming your cocktail glass with cinnamon and sugar!
2. Put your glass to the side and add ice to your shaker.
3. Add all the ingredients.
4. Shake cold!
5. Strain into your rimmed cocktail glass.
6. Serve!
ba-cable-car.description:
Tony Abou-Ganim, also known as The Modern Mixologist, is a bartending legend that co-founded the Starlight Room. He created the Cable Car cocktail to pay tribute to San Francisco's cable cars! The cable cars of San Francisco are an icon of a past era. They still climb the hills of San Francisco and carry commuters and tourists up and down busy streets.

This rum sour is sweet, tart, and lightly spiced, regardless of whether you are familiar with its name. The Cable Car cocktail is a modified Sidecar. It substitutes brandy with spiced rum, back then, spiced rum was very uncommon.

Abou-Ganim's original cocktails helped to establish San Francisco as a cocktail destination in an era that was defined by Cosmopolitan and other similar drinks.

Captain Morgan was probably the most widely available spiced rum label at the time of Cable Car's inception. The Captain is probably still the most well-known of the category, but today there are plenty of other options. A more luxurious approach is to maybe use something like a Boukman Botanical Rhum.

Similar to a Sidecar or Brandy Crusta, the Cable Car includes an orange liqueur in addition to simple syrup for sweetness--specifically, orange curacao. using Bol's or something similar can make the drink heavy, so it's better to use a dry curacao. Abou-Ganim uses Marie Brizard Orange Curacao in the original recipe. Grand Marnier or maybe Cointreau would also work great.

Another aspect that made the Cable Car a classic is the way it was presented. Abou-Ganim uses a mixture of cinnamon and sugar to give the drink a punchier sweetness and a present hint of spice.

ba-cafe-ireland.method_text: 1. Combine all of the ingredients with ice and stir very briefly, only for 5 seconds or so. Strain into the glass and serve.
ba-cafe-ireland.description: Likening this cocktail to a dry Irish whiskey Manhattan, Yanni Kehagiaras notes that the drinkshould be stirred very briefly with ice. “It’s about retaining the texture and viscosity,” says Kehagiaras, co-owner of Stoa in San Francisco, one of this year’s Imbibe 75 Places to Watch. “Just a brief chill and it’s good.”

ba-cafe-martini.method_text:
1. Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice
2. Shake and strain into the glass
ba-cafe-martini.description: At Saint Theo's in New York, beverage director Simon Sebbah elevates the Espresso Martini by trading out vodka for reposado tequila, giving it "a little extra kick and dimension."

ba-cafe-racer.method_text:
1. Add ingredients to a mixing glass with ice
2. Stir 20 seconds and strain into a chilled glass
3. Express an orange peel and garnish
ba-cafe-racer.description: A cold weather appropriate digestif, inspired by the delicious pairing of cacao, coffee, and raw cane sugar.

ba-calvados-tonic.method_text:
1. Pour the Calvados into a Burgundy glass over ice.
2. Top with tonic water.
3. Garnish with a lemon twist.
ba-calvados-tonic.description: The Calvados & Tonic is a staple in Normandy. Sarah Morrissey presents hers in a Burgundy glass with heaps of ice and a ton of tonic.

ingredients.name: Barbados Rum
ingredients.note: Armani/Ristorante 5th Avenue uses Mount Gay Eclipse

ba-calypso.method_text: 1. Add all of the ingredients to a shaker, add ice, then shake vigorously. Double-strain into a rocks glass with a large cube, then garnish.
ba-calypso.description: Named for the ship belonging to French ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau, this tropical port cocktail—combining rum from Barbados, tawny Port from Portugal, and bergamot liqueur from Italy—showcases the fortified wine's summery side.

ba-cameron-park-spritz.method_text: 1. Add the Aperol, elderflower liqueur, and mezcal to an ice-filled glass. Add a splash of sparkling water, then top with 2-3 oz. of sparkling wine. Garnish.
ba-cameron-park-spritz.description: Named after a Hispanic neighborhood in Brownsville, Texas, this Spritz incorporates flavors that nod to that heritage, says Christopher Galicia, beverage director and junior partner with Ramblas Hospitality Group. “Coming into summer, we wanted a spritz that was lively, floral, and had a little bit more backbone,” says Galicia. “Mezcal and St-Germain play these roles perfectly and produce a deliciously bold spritz.”

ba-campbeltown.method_text:
1. Add the Springbank 10-year-old scotch, Cherry Heering liqueur, and green Chartreuse into a mixing glass with ice and stir until well-chilled.
2. Strain into a chilled Nick & Nora glass.
3. Express the oil of a lemon peel over the drink and discard.
ba-campbeltown.description: Three ingredients add up to one perfect sip in this expensive and utterly delicious Scottish cocktail

ba-cane-tables-royal-hawaiian.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a shaker.
2. Add a handful of pebble ice and whip-shake.
3. Pour into a chilled double rocks glass, and top with more pebble ice.
4. Garnish with a mint bouquet and serve with a straw.
ba-cane-tables-royal-hawaiian.description: A tropical gin cocktail recipe, the Royal Hawaiian is reimagined at Cane & Table, where the pineapple drink is served on crushed ice.

ba-cantaritos.method_text:
1. If using the traditional clay cup for serving, soak it in cold water for 10 minutes before using. Otherwise, use a highball glass.
2. Combine the tequila, orange juice, lemon juice and lime juice in the glass with a pinch of salt.
3. Fill the glass with ice and top with grapefruit soda.
ba-cantaritos.description: Cantaritos are Mexican tequila cocktails served in clay cups! Similar to the Paloma, this drink stars grapefruit soda and citrus.

ingredients.name: Espresso
ingredients.note: cooled to room temperature or chilled

ba-carajillo.method_text:
1. Brew 3 oz. of espresso per drink and cool to room temperature or chill in
the fridge to prevent excess dilution. In a shaker filled with ice, add chilled espresso and Licor 43. Shake well until creamy and frothy, then strain into the glass filled with fresh ice, and garnish.
TIPThe Carajillo is as much a coffee drink as it is a cocktail—brewing the espresso fresh, and using a high-quality coffee, will have a big impact on the final flavor.
ba-carajillo.description: Bolstering one’s coffee with a shot of booze is more or less a universally accepted practice, regardless of time of day or occasion. The exact origins of Spain’s version, the Carajillo, remain up for debate. Some point to Spanish soldiers in Cuba adding rum to their coffee to muster the coraje needed for battle, while others have suggested the drink’s roots are in southern Spain’s Andalusia region, with the name derived from the Spanish expletive carajo. It’s perhaps a fitting sentiment while doctoring your cup—why not? The drink has since migrated overseas, becoming popular in Latin American countries and Mexico City in particular, where a Carajillo recipe can be found on virtually any bar menu. The go-to booze these days is also a Spanish export, Licor 43—a sweet, botanical liqueur with notes of vanilla and citrus—thanks to savvy marketing by the brand. The drink has been on the menu at Mexico City institution Contramar “since always,” notes operations director Armando Camacho. “However, it really became popular shortly after the pandemic, when the Licor 43 brand made a significant advertising effort.” The stateside popularity of Espresso Martinis and their ilk have extended an affinity for coffee-based cocktails more broadly, making the Carajillo cocktail a perfect two-ingredient fit for any hour of the day. “The acidity of the coffee goes very well with the sweetness of the liqueur. It’s perfect after an abundant meal,” says Camacho. “It often happens to us that a table full of people orders Carajillos, and the next table sees it and orders a round for themselves. It’s a cocktail that you crave when you see it."

ba-caribbean-ember-2.method_text:
1. Combine all of the ingredients except ginger beer in a cocktail shaker.
2. Add ice and shake until chilled.
3. Strain into a cocktail glass filled with ice.
4. Top with chilled ginger beer.
ba-caribbean-ember-2.description:
Tiki cocktails and whiskey is far from traditional cocktail combination. However, in Caribbean Ember Tyler Malone brings it together masterfully and with a great and delicious effect.

Cocktail is built around the blend of dark rum and rye whiskey. Dark rum contributes rich molasses, caramel, dried fruit notes, while whiskey adds some oaky, peppery spiciness, resulting in a one-of-a-kind cocktail base. Splash of pineapple juice, pays homage to the tiki culture with distinct sweet-tart fruitiness, while a touch of lime juice and maple syrup, expands the flavours of rum and whiskey. All of these notes are then wrapped up by the warming spiciness of ginger beer, providing not only freshness, but also balancing the cocktail out. A few dashes of Angostura bitters bring it all together and imparts more tropical notes bridging the gap between old-fashioned and tiki styles.

Caribbean Ember is a unique and intriguing cocktail. Many have tried to incorporate whiskey into a tropical drink, but most of these attempts have failed, Caribbean Ember is the rare exception.
ba-caribbean-ember-2.garnish: Garnish with a sprig of mint, lime wheel, pineapple spears and an edible flower.

ba-caribbean-parachute.method_text:
1. Add all of the ingredients except tonic water to a shaker with no ice.
2. Shake to combine, then add ice and shake well until chilled and foamy.
3. Add chilled tonic water to an empty Collins glass, then strain the cocktail into the tonic until the top of the drink is half an inch below the rim.
4. Wait for the foam to completely settle, then finish straining the remainder of the cocktail.
ba-caribbean-parachute.description: This rum and tonic adds the building blocks of a Silver Fizz and the balance of a rich amaro, resulting in a beautifully textured highball.

ba-ce-soir.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass over ice and stir until chilled.
2. Strain into a chilled coupe or cocktail glass.
3. Express the lemon peel and discard.
ba-ce-soir.description: A mix of Cognac, with touches of yellow Chartreuse and Cynar, and two types of bitters, this cocktail recipe is potent and elegant.

ba-celery-gin-sour.method_text: Muddle the celery with the lemon juice and simple, then shake with the gin and ice.

ba-central-park-to-lumphini.method_text: 1. Add all of the ingredients to a shaker with ice. Shake to chill and dump into a glass over a large ice cube. Garnish.
ba-central-park-to-lumphini.description: Tantai Khantachavana of BKK New York, a restaurant that blends Bangkok street food and New York cuisine, deliciously encapsulates the experience of an autumn stroll in his fig cocktail. Mezcal serves as an earthy foundation that's then layered with the baking spice notes of seasonal fruit.

ba-charles-dickens-punch.method_text:
1. A few hours before preparing the punch, peel 4 lemons with a vegetable peeler or paring knife to create 4 long spirals of peel. Put them in a heatproof bowl with 3/4 of a cup of demerara sugar. Muddle the peels and
the sugar together and let sit at room temperature. Juice the 4 peeled lemons (and any extra needed) through a strainer to yield 6 oz. of strained juice. Set aside in the fridge.
2. Measure the rum and Cognac into a pitcher or other pouring vessel. To prepare the punch, boil the water and place the bowl containing the lemon peels and sugar on a wooden cutting board or other heat-resistant surface in an open area (free from clutter, flammable items, or nearby curtains or light fixtures) where everyone can gather around at a safe distance.
3. Pour the Cognac and rum into the bowl. Use a long-handled barspoon to remove a spoonful of the rum-cognac mixture. Light the spoonful on fire with a match and hold it just above the surface of the bowl in order to ignite the rest of the liquid. Stir with the barspoon or a heatproof ladle to help dissolve the sugar. Let the mixture burn for 2 or 3 minutes, occasionally lifting out one of the lemon peels with the ladle or spoon to show the flames running down it.
4. Cover the bowl with a large heatproof dish or tray to extinguish the flames. Add the lemon juice and the hot water. (For cold punch, replace the hot water with 3 cups of cold water and add a 1-quart block of ice, made by freezing a quart bowl of water for 24 hours.) Stir. Grate fresh nutmeg over the top and ladle out in 3-ounce servings.
ba-charles-dickens-punch.description: “Dickens was a dedicated punch-maker and an inveterate showman,” says drinks historian David Wondrich, offering as proof this historic flaming punch from his 2010 book Punch: The Delights (and Dangers) of the Flowing Bowl. And with a simple list of ingredients and some fireproof tools, you, too, can add some razzle dazzle to your own holiday gathering. Be sure to use a heatproof bowl with a capacity of at least one gallon.

ba-chauncey.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
2. Stir until chilled.
3. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
4. Garnish with a lemon or orange twist.
ba-chauncey.description: Equal-parts gin, Cognac and rye whiskey with sweet vermouth and orange bitters make up this historic cocktail recipe.

ba-chocolate-martica.method_text: Stir all of the ingredients with ice, then strain into a chilled glass.
ba-chocolate-martica.description: This simple variation on a Death & Co modern classic from 2007 was one of the first to tap chocolate bitters’ flavor potential.

ba-chrysanthemum.method_text:
1. Stir all of the ingredients in a mixing glass with ice until chilled. Strain into a chilled glass and garnish.
2. Tip“I would also try this with blanc vermouth, as many of the recipes of this era like the Algonquin, El Presidente, and Blackthorn that call for dry vermouth taste better with blanc vermouth, in my opinion,” notes Meehan.
ba-chrysanthemum.description: Hard to spell but easy to drink, the Chrysanthemum falls into the category of lesser-known classics—still held in good regard, but not often invited to the party. However, with a formula that ticks the current trendy cocktail boxes, the Chrysanthemum might just be ready to bloom once more. Debuting more than a century ago, the recipe first appeared in Hugo Ensslin’s Recipes for Mixed Drinks in 1916, followed by an adaptation by Harry Craddock in 1930 for The Savoy Cocktail Book. Eschewing a base spirit altogether, the Chrysanthemum puts vermouth in the spotlight, augmented with herbal liqueur Bénédictine and boosted by a few dashes of absinthe. “When absinthe was legalized [in the U.S.] at the end of 2006, a lot of bartenders went looking for golden age recipes to see what we could do with the newly legalized spirit,” says bartender and author Jim Meehan, pointing to the drink’s initial resurgence within the craft cocktail renaissance. The primary variation is seen in the ratio of the cocktail, evolving over thedecades in step with drinkers’ tastes. While Ensslin’s early recipe called for equal parts dry vermouth and Bénédictine, Craddock’s version dialed back the sweetness with a 2:1 ratio, which remains more or less the standard today. “The key to resurrecting recipes like this is bringing the big flavors into balance and bringing the sweetness down from the original formula,” says Meehan. “Adding more dry vermouth also throttles the strength of the drink, which makes it more appealing for the aperitif audience. The recipe is a delicious puzzle, with much complexity to consider.

ba-ciderhouse-mule.method_text:
1. Add all of the ingredients, except the sparkling rosé, to a shaker with ice.
2. Shake until chilled.
3. Add the sparkling rosé to the shaker before straining the cocktail into a glass filled with ice.
4. Garnish.
ba-ciderhouse-mule.description: Taking the Moscow Mule into spritz territory, Tim Sweeney, head bartender of Pebble Bar in New York City, combines vodka, lime, and ginger syrup with a touch of raspberry liqueur and sparkling rosé.

ba-cinder-bloom.method_text: 1. Place 4 ají dulce peppers in a shaker and muddle. Add the rest of the ingredients along with ice. Shake hard for about 5 seconds, or until the outside of the shaker is frosty. Strain into the glass over ice.
ba-cinder-bloom.description: "The inspiration behind this cocktail began with my love for the Margarita," says Omar Bautista, beverage manager of Boro Brine in New York City. Using the tequila classic as a template, he layered the bold flavors of passion fruit and Aperol with the sweet vegetal notes of ají peppers for a refreshing and aromatic cocktail. Bautista says that any tropical pepper will work, too, or swap in red or yellow bell peppers for a more vegetal profile.

ba-clarified-new-york-sour.method_text:
1. Combine the bourbon, lemon, and simple syrup and pour over the milk in a glass container.
2. Let sit for 30 minutes, allowing the milk to curdle.
3. Strain the milk mixture through a coffee filter.
4. If it’s not clear, re-pour through the same filter.
5. To serve, pour the mixture over a large ice cube in a glass.
6. Float with red wine.
ba-clarified-new-york-sour.description: This clarified take on the New York Sour achieves a silky mouthfeel and a softened acidity, making for an easy-drinking sipper. "I’m always looking for ways to use fun techniques to make twists on classic cocktails," says Prohibition bar manager Jim McCourt. "I also like the presentation of the contrasting colors."

ba-clover-leaf.method_text:
1. Combine the Chambord or grenadine, lemon juice, egg white or half-and-half, and gin in a cocktail shaker with ice cubes.
2. Shake vigorously for 10 seconds, until the ingredients are cold and the mix is frothy with a pink blush.
3. Strain into a Martini or coupe cocktail glass, making sure there is a thin layer of foam and a few small ice chips floating on top.
4. Garnish with the mint leaf.
ba-clover-leaf.description: This recipe from James Beard Award-winning culinary historian and journalist Toni Tipton-Martin is a modern take on a century-old relative of the Clover Club cocktail, utilizing a base of gin and Chambord to create a berry-forward delight.

ba-coffee-cigarettes.method_text:
1. Combine the ingredients into your mixing glass
2. Stir with ice for 30-40 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled stemmed cocktail glass
ba-coffee-cigarettes.description: The Coffee & Cigarettes cocktail was created by Thomas Waugh and featured in the Death & Co. cocktail book. This riff on a Manhattan / Rob Roy features an Islay Whisky which provides a rich smokiness that compliments the coffee & cacao notes.I highly recommend trying this one!

ba-coffee-cocktail.method_text:
1. Combine all of the ingredients in a cocktail shaker.
2. Dry shake to emulsify the egg.
3. Add ice and shake until chilled.
4. Double strain into a chilled cocktail glass.
ba-coffee-cocktail.description:
It probably would be difficult to come up with a more misleading name for this cocktail, than Coffee Cocktail. It does not feature coffee or have anything in common with it, unless you consider coffee to be delicious (which I do by the way) and this cocktail is certainly also delicious to the very last drop.

Base of this cocktail is Tawny Port, the aged nature of wine bringing notes of nuts, dried fruits and hint of rich sweetness. It is then paired with oak and vanilla tones of the cognac, increasing the overall cocktail complexity, while at the same time increasing proof. As a true flip requires, a whole egg is added, turning this cocktail into what it is, a rich and decadent indulgence. The creamy texture makes this cocktail especially suited for the holiday season. In the end, a touch of simple syrup helps with the balance and enables delicious individual notes pop to the forefront, while freshly grated nutmeg garnish adds a further aromatic dimension.

All in all, Coffee Cocktail might not have anything in common with its namesake, but it is a tasty and decadent drink, seemingly made for the holiday season.
ba-coffee-cocktail.garnish: Garnish with some freshly grated nutmeg.

ba-coffee-enzoni.method_text:
1. In a cocktail shaker, muddle the grapes
2. Add the remaining ingredients
3. Shake with ice for 10-12 seconds
4. Double strain over ice into an old fashioned glass
5. Garnish with 3 skewered black grapes
ba-coffee-enzoni.description: The Enzoni is a personal favorite of mine. I first shared it in 2020 and the video has received almost 700,000 views (other people love it too!). I also featured it more recently in my top 3 cocktails video a few weeks ago before stumbling across Dan Fellows' caffeinated version. I knew I had to try it immediately and it did not disappoint!The Coffee Enzoni is a pretty straight forward variation on the original Enzoni with the use of black grapes (sable grapes if available) instead of green, and the addition of coffee liqueur. Whilst the original Enzoni is bright and bitter, the Coffee Enzoni is dark, rich and brooding. It features rich bitter coffee notes and a juicy, muscat grape flavor.Worth noting... Dan used an extra dry coffee liqueur with 100g of sugar per litre. Mr Black has 250g per litre. For comparison, Kahlua has 400g per litre. As a result, he adds 10 ml of a 2:1 light muscovado syrup to balance the drink. Because I used Mr Black, the additional syrup isn't required.

ba-coffee-julep.method_text:
1. Muddle 5-10 mint leaves with syrup in a julep cup
2. Fill with crushed ice and add bourbon and coffee liqueur
3. Stir until cold and frosty, then top with more crushed ice
4. Smack a mint sprig between your hands to express its oils, then garnish
ba-coffee-julep.description: Coffee liqueur and Demerara Gum Syrup give this Julep a jolt of rich flavor.

ba-coffee-negroni.method_text: Stir all ingredients in an ice-filled mixing glass, then strain into an ice-filled rocks glass
ba-coffee-negroni.description: It’s commonly been said that the only thing better than a Negroni is a Coffee Negroni. And considering the drink is an equal part mix of Coffee Liqueur, Campari & Gin, we’ve got to agree.

ba-comte-de-sureau.method_text: Stir with ice and strain into a chilled rocks glass over ice.
ba-comte-de-sureau.description: The name translates to count of elderflower, which is a nod to the St-Germain that acts as the floral sweetener here.
ba-comte-de-sureau.garnish: Garnish with orange and lemon twists.

ba-conference-cocktail.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice
2. Stir 20 seconds and strain into a chilled rocks glass with ice.
ba-conference-cocktail.description: Tiki was jealous of the Old Fashioned build, and the Conference cocktail was born. From Brian Miller at Death & Co.

ba-coronado-cocktail.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 10 seconds
3. Strain into a highball glass over crushed ice
4. Garnish with a lemon wheel
ba-coronado-cocktail.description: The combination of Tropical Passionfruit Syrup, coconut water, and tequila has tropical written all over it. The Coronado Cocktail was made by Chris Santos and found in his bookShare: Delicious and Surprising Recipes to Pass Around Your Table.

ba-cosa-nostra-2.method_text:
Shake everything except the ginger ale with ice and strain into a pilsner glass over crushed ice.
Top with the ginger ale
ba-cosa-nostra-2.description: A delicious and simple Highball created by Dane Barca at Smuggler's Cove

ingredients.name: Vermouth Bianco
ingredients.note: Somssi uses a 50/50 blend of Noilly Prat Extra Dry and Cocchi Americano Bianco

ba-countermand.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a chilled, petite glass with one large ice cube.
2. Stir briefly, then express a lemon coin over the drink and discard.
ba-countermand.description: The Countermand is a mini reverse Martini cocktail recipe served at the NYC restaurant Somssi. It's made with gin, maraschino and absinthe.

ba-creole-gimlet.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a shaker and shake.
2. Double strain into a chilled Coupe glass.
3. Garnish with lime wheel.
ba-creole-gimlet.description: Falernum adds hints of Caribbean Island flavors for a tasty twist on the classic Gimlet. The touch of Caribbean spice makes you want to dance to island music.

ba-cucumber-gimlet.method_text: Combine all ingredients and shake with ice. Serve in a rocks glass over crushed ice. Garnish with a rolled cucumber slice.

ba-cynar-flip.method_text:
1. Dry shake the whole egg in a cocktail shaker
2. Add Cynar, simple syrup, and ice before shaking again
3. Strain into a cocktail glass and drop several dashes of the bitters into the foam
ba-cynar-flip.description: A magnificent application of Cynar in the holiday canon

ba-daiquiri-4.method_text:
1. Blend all ingredients with a scoop of crushed ice for 15 seconds.
2. Pour into an 8 1/2-ounce coupe glass.
3. Serve with straws.
ba-daiquiri-4.description: A frozen Daiquiri cocktail recipe from Cafe La Trova, also known as the Hemingway Daiquiri, after the author who was known to drink them.

ingredients.name: Dark Rum
ingredients.note: such as Worthy Park 109 Dark Jamaican Rum

ingredients.name: Crème de banane
ingredients.note: such as Giffard Banane du Brasil

ba-day-o-fashioned.method_text:
1. In a rocks glass, muddle the orange peel with the bitters.
2. Add the rest of the ingredients and ice, and stir gently until well-chilled.
3. Garnish with an orange slice and a black cherry.
ba-day-o-fashioned.description: The Day-O’ Fashioned is a tropical Old-Fashioned cocktail recipe made with rye whiskey, rum, banana liqueur, cold brew, orange and Angostura.

ba-dead-mans-handle.method_text: Combine, Shake with Ice. Top with a sprinkle of Tajín seasoning.
ba-dead-mans-handle.description: This summery tequila cocktail from Tiffany Kirk at Miss Carousel in Houston gets punched up with Aperol and perfectly sweetened with orgeat.

ba-dead-sea-mule.method_text:
1. Fill a Collins glass with ice, then add the mezcal, lime juice and grenadine.
2. Top with the ginger beer and stir briefly and gently to combine.
3. Garnish with the mint sprig and 2 skewered pieces of candied ginger.
ba-dead-sea-mule.description: A house-made pomegranate grenadine is the key to the Dead Sea Mule, a mezcal-laced twist on the classic Moscow Mule.

ba-death-flip.method_text: 1. Combine all ingredients in a mixing tin and shake with ice. Strain into a sour glass.
ba-death-flip.description:
When this cocktail first appeared on the menu at the Black Pearl in Melbourne, in 2010, no ingredients were listed. And if you asked what was in the drink, the bartender would not tell you. The only thing offering the customer a hint as to what they were getting into was the ominous description: “You don’t wanna meet this cocktail in a dark alley.”

Of course, plenty of people stepped up to take the bait, and many ended up liking the cocktail—something that likely wouldn’t have happened if the ingredients were listed: tequila, yellow Chartreuse, Jägermeister and a whole egg. To date, it is the only flip to become a modern classic.

ba-debbie-dont.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients over ice and shake
2. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass, serve up
ba-debbie-dont.description: An adventurous modern cocktail for those with a limited bar

ba-deep-south.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker
2. Add ice and shake hard for 20 seconds
3. Strain into a chilled rocks glass
ba-deep-south.description: Our peach syrup, with a split base of mezcal and rye whiskey, adds a summer note to this whiskey sour.

ba-delta-t.method_text:
1. Add all ingredients except ginger beer to a shaking tin.
2. Add ice and shake until chilled.
3. Strain into a highball glass over an ice spear.
4. Top with ginger beer.
5. Add several dashes of Angostura bitters on top.
ba-delta-t.description: A cocktail designed to highlight the unique buttery and funky notes of Variable Dunderclap rum, balanced by the sharpness of ginger and the herbaceous qualities of Fernet. It's a complex, easy-sipping drink that plays with contrasts of hot and cold flavors.
ba-delta-t.garnish: candied ginger, lime peel, and a fresh bunch of mint

ba-diki-diki.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients over ice and shake
2. Strain into a chilled cocktail glass, serve up
ba-diki-diki.description: A revived golden-era cocktail and fabulous way to tinker with Swedish Punsch

ba-dirty-martini.method_text:
1. Select and pre-chill a Martini glass.
2. Prepare garnish of skewered Green Olives.
3. Stir all ingredients with ice.
4. Strain into chilled glass.
5. Garnish with skewered olives.
ba-dirty-martini.description: The Dirty Martini is a popular cocktail that adds olive brine to the classic Martini, giving it a savory flavor. It can be made with either gin or vodka, depending on personal preference.

ba-disgruntled-mai-tai.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients except for the Underberg in a cocktail shaker.
2. Briefly dry shake without ice, then add a few small ice cubes and shake until the ice has melted.
3. Pour into a chilled rocks glass and top with crushed ice.
4. Remove the cap and the top of the paper wrapper on the Underberg bottle and insert it, upside-down, into the crushed ice.
5. Garnish with a mint sprig, lime wedge, grated nutmeg and a cocktail umbrella.
ba-disgruntled-mai-tai.description: The Disgruntled Mai Tai is a spin on the rum tiki drink that adds Aperol and a bottle of bitter Underberg to the cocktail.
ba-disgruntled-mai-tai.garnish: mint sprig, lime wedge, freshly grated nutmeg, cocktail umbrella

ba-division-bell.method_text:
1. Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice and shake until chilled.
2. Strain into a coupe.
3. Express a grapefruit twist over the surface of the drink, then discard.
ba-division-bell.description: Mezcal takes the place of gin and Aperol that of Chartreuse in this simple riff on the Last Word.

ba-don-lockwood.method_text:
1. In a mixing glass combine all ingredients
2. Stir with ice for 20-30 seconds
3. Strain over ice into an old fashioned glass
